\section[nadi]{\te{నది} (nadi) — a river}

\label{lesson:TE-C55-river}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{mokka} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{నది}}
\textbf{\te{నది}} (\emph{nadi}) — \textquotedblleft{}a river\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{nadī} is the river, and it is built on a piece meaning \textquotedblleft{}to sound, to roar\textquotedblright{}. A river is named for the noise it makes, which tells you the people who named it were listening for water before they could see it.

Telugu clipped the long final vowel and says \te{నది}. The inherited Telugu word is \te{ఏరు}, a stream, and it survives in place names up and down the country long after it stopped being said on its own.

\te{నది} is the word you want when asking a stranger which way the water is.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first thing you would ask the way to.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nadi}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{nadi}, then \emph{dayacēsi}, and put the two together as a question
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{నది} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a river\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ceruvu]{\te{చెరువు} (ceruvu) — a village tank, a reservoir}

\label{lesson:TE-C55-tank}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{nadi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{చెరువు}}
\textbf{\te{చెరువు}} (\emph{ceruvu}) — \textquotedblleft{}a village tank, a reservoir\textquotedblright{}.

A \te{చెరువు} is not a natural lake. It is a dug and banked tank that catches the rain and holds it through the dry months, and a great many Telugu villages were laid out around one before they were laid out around anything else.

So the word carries an argument about how the country was settled: the \te{నది} is where the water goes, the \te{చెరువు} is where it was made to stay. Kings had them dug and put their names on the bunds, and the names are still there.

Indian English calls this a \textquotedblleft{}tank\textquotedblright{}, which is why the translation can sound strange until you have stood on the bund of one.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two waters: one that moves, one that was kept.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ceruvu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{ceruvu}, then \emph{nadi}, and say which one people made
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{చెరువు} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a village tank, a reservoir\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[guṭṭa]{\te{గుట్ట} (guṭṭa) — a low hill}

\label{lesson:TE-C55-hill}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{ceruvu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{గుట్ట}}
\textbf{\te{గుట్ట}} (\emph{guṭṭa}) — \textquotedblleft{}a low hill\textquotedblright{}.

\te{గుట్ట} is inherited, and it means the small rocky rise that the Deccan is covered in — a heap of boulders rather than a peak. It also means a heap of anything: a \te{గుట్ట} of grain, a \te{గుట్ట} of clothes.

That double sense is honest about the landscape. These hills look piled rather than pushed up, and a speaker naming one is naming a pile.

The borrowed \te{పర్వతం} is the big mountain, the one in a poem. Nobody calls the rise behind their village a \te{పర్వతం}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three: water that moves, water that stays, and ground that stands up.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{guṭṭa}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{guṭṭa}, then \emph{ceruvu}, and say which of the two you would climb
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{గుట్ట} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a low hill\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[grāmaṁ]{\te{గ్రామం} (grāmaṁ) — a village}

\label{lesson:TE-C55-village}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{guṭṭa} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{గ్రామం}}
\textbf{\te{గ్రామం}} (\emph{grāmaṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a village\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{grāma} began as the word for a moving band of people, a travelling group, and settled into meaning the place they settled in. The word sat down when the people did.

Telugu's own word is \emph{ūru}, and it is the one used in speech: it is in half the place names on the map and it is what you say to a neighbour. \te{గ్రామం} is the official register — the word on a form, in a land record, on a signboard.

So a Telugu speaker holds two villages, one for the revenue office and one for home.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{grāmaṁ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{grāmaṁ}, then \emph{ceruvu}, and say which one a village is built around
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{గ్రామం} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a village\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bāṭa]{\te{బాట} (bāṭa) — a path, a way}

\label{lesson:TE-C55-path}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{grāmaṁ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{బాట}}
\textbf{\te{బాట}} (\emph{bāṭa}) — \textquotedblleft{}a path, a way\textquotedblright{}.

\te{బాట} is the inherited word for a way, a track, the line worn by feet going the same way twice. \te{దారి} does much the same work; \te{బాట} is the more physical of the two, the ground itself.

It goes abstract as easily as English \textquotedblleft{}path\textquotedblright{} does. \te{బాట} \te{పట్టు} is to take up a way of living, and a person can be on somebody else's \te{బాట}.

You can now ask your way properly: \te{దయచేసి}, which \te{గ్రామం}, which \te{బాట}, which side the \te{నది} is on.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \te{నది}, \te{చెరువు}, \te{గుట్ట}, \te{గ్రామం}, \te{బాట}. Enough to be given directions with.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bāṭa}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then ask a stranger the way to the \te{నది} using \emph{dayacēsi}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{బాట} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a path, a way\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
